Q: Situations where R strips attributes for S3 classes, and how to work around or avoid them? A:

Hmm, maybe I could choose something like NA, where losing the class will cause immediate and obvious errors to make the user aware something has gone wrong.

If there's not really a "safe" failure case possible for the class, the next-best thing would be one that makes it extremely obvious. And then clear documentation explaining what causes it and how to avoid it.

Edit: No, that won't work either, apparently subsetting removes attributes other than name and class. So you're right, I have to make the value the actual value and not hide it in an attribute.

Sounds like I need to rethink this whole idea. Given that the user could accidentally strip the class away at any time, I don't think it's safe for it to use methods to hide all the logarithm stuff from the user and pretend to be a double when it's not.

Q: Pickling error work-around when passing decorators to multiprocessing module A:

Thanks to @Sébastien Guarnay for the great solution to my question. Using partial may be the perfect way to create "parameterized" functions. In reading up on partial, I also learned of a new feature in Python 3.14 - the functools.Placeholder. This allows for flexibility in where to place the fixed "parameters" vs. variables.

Other advantages of partial

  • Almost twice as fast as alternatives (see below). For example, partial is faster than using a class with a defined __call__ function**.**

  • functions created using partial can be passed to multiprocessing processes without any pickling errors. In fact, partial functions can be created locally, and still avoid pickling errors.

  • Requires less code than alternatives (class, decorator).

  • The Placeholder allows for more natural arrangement of arguments in many cases, and doesn't produce any cost overhead.

See some examples below

from dataclasses import dataclass
from functools import partial, Placeholder, wraps

from math import cos

def f_trig(x,m):
    return cos(m*x)

def fwrap(f,qname,*args):
    @wraps(f)
    def wrapper(x):
        return f(x,*args)
    wrapper.__qualname__ = qname
    return wrapper

@dataclass
class c_trig:
    m : int
    def __call__(self,x):
        return f_trig(x,self.m)

# "Decorator"
f1 = fwrap(f_trig,'f1',m:=2)

# Class
f2 = c_trig(m)

# from functools
_x = Placeholder
f3 = partial(f_trig,_x,m)


print(f1(2))
print(f2(2))
print(f3(2))
print("")

print("Using original decorator idea")
%timeit f1(2)
print("")

print("Using dataclass object")
%timeit f2(2)
print("")

print("Using partial")
%timeit f3(2)
print("")

Timing results :

-0.6536436208636119
-0.6536436208636119
-0.6536436208636119

Using original decorator idea
163 ns ± 1.08 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000,000 loops each)

Using dataclass object
131 ns ± 0.61 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000,000 loops each)

Using partial
92.1 ns ± 0.574 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 10,000,000 loops each)

partial is about 1.8x speed-up over my original decorator idea and about 1.4x speed-up over using a callable class object.

Q: How to parse informal Persian number words into an integer currency value (Rial) A:

First thing to know: how big would be the dictionary of all the number words, taking into account all the forms and variants?

If the dictionary is not too short to bother, it may makes sense to consider the approach based on the agglutinative nature of Persian. How big would be the dictionary of the roots, prefixes, and suffixes related to the the number words? In this approach, how many composition rules should be applied to compose all thinkable number words?

Without this initial estimate, it would be hard to consider and compare best strategies for recognition of numbers expressed via words. In some languages, even this highly simplified text parsing problem could be pretty complicated.

Q: Setting `isDebuggable true` in Android buildTypes-->debug results in gradle sync error A:

isDebuggable is true for debug and is false for release build variant by default (source). You can customise it as shown in the documentation:

// for build.gradle.kts
isDebuggable = true

// for build.gradle
debuggable true

So, you need to use debuggable instead of isDebuggable because you are using Groovy now.

Q: gRPC DNS resolution failed when using machine name A:

Thanks to @jdweng for pointing me in the right direction, this was solved by adding the DNS suffix to the hostname (skylake.lan in my case). We can get the DNS suffix via IPInterfaceProperties.DnsSuffix.

Alternatively, (which might be safer) we can use the correct IP address instead of the host name by using something like that.
